opus-5.5.text:
That's a really good question, and I think the distinction is subtler than it first appears.

When you're solving an ARC puzzle, you're given a handful of input-output examples, and you're essentially running simulations in your head. You hypothesize a rule ("oh, the blue objects move until they hit a wall"), then you mentally apply it to the examples and check whether it reproduces what you see. That's a kind of experiment, but it's an experiment on your *own model*, not on the world. You're interrogating your hypotheses against fixed data. You can't go back and ask the puzzle a new question. You can't say, "What would happen if I put a red square here instead?"

Interaction with a real-world system is different in a fundamental way: you get to intervene. You choose the input, and the world tells you what happens. That's the difference between observational and interventional reasoning in the causal sense. With intervention, you can design experiments that discriminate between hypotheses that are indistinguishable from passive data. In ARC, if two rules both explain all the examples, you're stuck relying on priors, simplicity, or some notion of what the puzzle designer "meant." In the real world, you can go poke at the thing until one of those hypotheses breaks.

That said, I don't want to draw the line too sharply, because the mental experiments matter enormously. Humans are very good at simulating interventions internally before they act. A scientist doesn't run every possible experiment; they imagine outcomes under competing theories and pick the experiment that would be most informative. So the internal simulation is what makes real-world experimentation efficient. ARC exercises that imaginative capacity, but it cuts it off from the feedback loop that makes it really powerful.

That's part of why I've been interested in moving toward more interactive settings: environments where an agent has to figure out the rules by acting, not just by staring at examples. Then you can actually measure whether a system is curious in the right way. Does it take actions that resolve its uncertainty? Does it build a model it can reuse? Static benchmarks can't really test that, and I think it's a big piece of what we mean by general intelligence. It's not just inducing a rule from data; it's knowing how to go out and *get* the data that tells you which rule is right.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that in the ARC case, the thing you're interacting with isn't the world, it's a model of the world that you've already constructed. When I look at a puzzle and I think, "okay, what if I flip this shape, what if I treat these blue cells as a container," what I'm doing is running a simulation inside my head. I'm proposing a hypothesis, I'm playing it forward, and I'm checking whether the output matches the examples I've been given. That is an experiment in a meaningful sense. You have a hypothesis, you have an intervention, you have an outcome. But the system you're intervening on is one that you built, and so the thing you can learn from it is bounded by the fidelity of that internal model.

With a real-world system, the key difference is that the world can surprise you. You poke it and it does something you did not anticipate, and that surprise is the most informative signal you can get. In the mental experiment, surprise is possible but it's a weaker form. It's more like you discover a consequence of your own assumptions that you hadn't worked out yet. It's closer to a mathematician proving a theorem than a physicist running an apparatus.

That said, I don't think the line is as sharp as people sometimes want it to be. In ARC, there is a ground truth, the test output, and that acts as a kind of proxy for reality. You get feedback. The puzzle designer has an intent, and you're trying to reverse engineer it. So I'd actually describe what happens as a loop: you do a bunch of cheap, fast, internal simulation to prune the space of hypotheses, and then you spend your expensive interactions with the actual system, in this case checking against the examples or submitting an answer, very sparingly. And that's exactly the structure I think a good agent should have. Most reasoning is imagination, and then you occasionally touch the world to recalibrate.

The thing I find interesting, and part of why ARC appeals to me, is that it isolates the imagination part. It strips away the sensor noise and the actuator problems, and asks: given a handful of observations, how good is your ability to construct candidate world models and run them forward? That's the piece that I think is undertested in current systems. They're very good at retrieving, less good at genuinely composing a new mechanism in their head and seeing what it does.

astra-6.text:
I think the distinction is in what you’re interacting with. When I’m solving an ARC problem, I can entertain a hypothesis—perhaps this object moves until it hits that boundary—and mentally run it to see what would happen. I’m intervening on a model in my head. The result tells me something about the consequences of that hypothesis, but it doesn’t independently establish that the hypothesis is right.

With a real-world system, I can take an action and get an observation that isn’t determined by my model. The world can surprise me. So both involve this loop of proposing something, intervening, and examining the consequences, but the source of feedback is different. In ARC, the given examples constrain my interpretation; the mental experiments help me explore what that interpretation implies.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the distinction is less sharp than it might first appear. When I’m solving an ARC task, I might imagine that an object moves across the grid, or that a particular color acts as a barrier. I’m running a little experiment in my head: if this were the rule, what would happen? Then I compare that prediction with the examples.

With a real-world system, I can actually intervene and observe what happens. And the world can surprise me in ways that my mental simulation can’t, because my simulation is constrained by what I already understand. So mental experiments are useful for generating and exploring hypotheses, but they don’t independently establish that those hypotheses are correct.

In ARC, you have this very restricted interface: a few input-output examples, and you have to infer the transformation. You can experiment with your interpretation of those examples, but you generally can’t ask the underlying system for the output of an arbitrary new input. That makes the relationship between imagination and evidence particularly important.
